content:
# Deuteronomy Chapter 29 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA | 29 verses (Moab covenant)

---

## V.1 — Versification and opening line

- **EMET:** Verse 1 = "These are the words of the covenant that the LORD commanded Moshe to make with the sons of Yisra'el in the land of Moav..." (what English Bibles call 28:69, followed by a verse-2 opening of Moses's speech)
- **LOGOS:** Verse 1 = "Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: 'You have seen all that the LORD did...'" (LOGOS skips the Hebrew 29:1 superscription entirely; its ch. 29 opens with Moses's speech)
- **PNEUMA:** Verse 1 = "These are the terms of the covenant the LORD commanded Moses to make with the Israelites in Moab, in addition to the covenant he had made with them at Horeb." (follows MT versification like EMET)

**Differences:** EMET and PNEUMA include the superscription as v.1, following MT Hebrew chapter division. LOGOS omits it entirely and opens with Moses's speech, effectively one verse behind in numbering for the whole chapter. This is a structural disagreement affecting every verse number. **Resolution:** Follow MT versification (EMET/PNEUMA) — the superscription "These are the words of the covenant" is a genuine verse in the MT and its inclusion as v.1 is theologically significant as it distinguishes the Moab covenant from Horeb.

---

## V.1 — "Sons of Israel" vs. "Israel" vs. "Israelites"

- **EMET:** "the sons of Yisra'el" (b'nei Yisra'el)
- **LOGOS:** (verse absent from LOGOS due to versification shift)
- **PNEUMA:** "the Israelites"

**Differences:** EMET preserves the literal Hebrew b'nei Yisra'el. PNEUMA uses the idiomatic English "Israelites." **Resolution:** "the sons of Israel" — EMET; preserves the covenantal genealogical formula consistent with the project's convention for this phrase.

---

## V.1/2 — "Called" vs. "summoned"

- **EMET:** "And Moshe called to all Yisra'el and said to them" (v.2 in EMET)
- **LOGOS:** "Moses summoned all Israel and said to them" (v.1 in LOGOS)
- **PNEUMA:** "Moses summoned all the Israelites and said to them" (v.2 in PNEUMA)

**Differences:** EMET: "called to" (yiqra); LOGOS/PNEUMA: "summoned." The Hebrew qara el means "called to" — EMET is more literal. LOGOS/PNEUMA's "summoned" implies a formal convocation. **Resolution:** "And Moses called to all Israel and said to them" — EMET; "called to" is accurate and the verb qara does not carry the institutional weight that "summoned" implies.

---

## V.2/3 — "Your own eyes have seen" vs. "You have seen"

- **EMET:** "You have seen all that the LORD did before your eyes in the land of Mitsrayim"
- **LOGOS:** "You have seen all that the LORD did before your eyes in the land of Egypt"
- **PNEUMA:** "Your own eyes have seen everything the LORD did in Egypt to Pharaoh, to all his officials, and to all his land."

**Differences:** PNEUMA adds "Your own eyes" for emphasis — the Hebrew 'attem re'item is simply "you saw," with the pronoun giving stress. PNEUMA also renders "officials" for avadim (servants/slaves) and drops the phrase "before your eyes" in favor of the opening emphasis. EMET/LOGOS: "all his servants"; PNEUMA: "all his officials." The Hebrew avadim is "servants/slaves" not "officials." **Resolution:** "You have seen all that the LORD did before your eyes in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land" — EMET/LOGOS; "servants" is the correct rendering for avadim and "before your eyes" should be retained.

---

## V.3/4 — "Heart to understand" vs. "mind that understands"

- **EMET:** "Yet the LORD has not given you a heart to understand, or eyes to see, or ears to hear, until this day."
- **LOGOS:** "But to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear."
- **PNEUMA:** "But to this day the LORD has not given you a mind that understands or eyes that see or ears that hear."

**Differences:** (1) EMET/LOGOS: "a heart to understand" (lev lada'at — "a heart to know"); PNEUMA: "a mind that understands." The Hebrew lev is consistently rendered "heart" in this project and its cognitive-volitional meaning is captured by "heart to understand." PNEUMA's shift to "mind" flattens the Hebrew anthropology. (2) EMET: "Yet the LORD has not given" — temporal contrast with "yet"; LOGOS: "But to this day" — temporal marker at front; PNEUMA follows LOGOS on position. (3) EMET places "until this day" at the end; LOGOS/PNEUMA integrate "to this day" into the introduction. **Resolution:** "But to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand, or eyes to see, or ears to hear" — LOGOS structure, EMET/LOGOS vocabulary; "heart" over "mind."

---

## V.4/5 — "Garments did not wear out" vs. "clothes have not worn out" vs. "clothes did not wear out"

- **EMET:** "your garments did not wear out on you, and your sandal did not wear out on your foot"
- **LOGOS:** "Your clothes have not worn out on you, and your sandals have not worn off your feet"
- **PNEUMA:** "your clothes did not wear out, nor did the sandals on your feet"

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "garments" (simlah — outer garment/cloak); LOGOS/PNEUMA: "clothes." "Garments" is more precise for simlah. (2) EMET: singular "sandal" (na'alkha) and "foot" (raglekha) — following the Hebrew singular; LOGOS/PNEUMA: pluralize. The Hebrew uses the singular distributively. (3) LOGOS: "have not worn out" — present-perfect stative; EMET/PNEUMA: "did not wear out" — simple past. **Resolution:** "your garments did not wear out on you, and your sandal did not wear out on your foot" — EMET; the singular is deliberate Hebrew idiom, and "garments" is more precise.

---

## V.5/6 — "Bread you did not eat" vs. word order inversion

- **EMET:** "Bread you did not eat, and wine and strong drink you did not drink — so that you might know that I am the LORD your God."
- **LOGOS:** "You have not eaten bread, and you have not drunk wine or strong drink, so that you might know that I am the LORD your God."
- **PNEUMA:** "You ate no bread and drank no wine or other fermented drink. I did this so you would know that I am the LORD your God."

**Differences:** (1) EMET preserves the Hebrew fronted-noun word order ("Bread you did not eat") for rhetorical emphasis. LOGOS/PNEUMA use standard English syntax. (2) EMET/LOGOS: "strong drink" (shechar); PNEUMA: "other fermented drink" — a paraphrase. (3) PNEUMA adds "I did this" — an interpretive addition not in the Hebrew ("lema'an da'at" = "in order that you might know"). **Resolution:** "Bread you did not eat, and wine and strong drink you did not drink — so that you might know that I am the LORD your God" — EMET; fronted word order is rhetorically significant and "strong drink" is the established rendering for shechar.

---

## V.6/7 — "Came out to meet us" vs. "came out against us"

- **EMET:** "Sichon the king of Cheshbon and 'Og the king of Bashan came out to meet us for battle"
- **LOGOS:** "Sihon the king of Heshbon and Og the king of Bashan came out against us for battle"
- **PNEUMA:** "Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan came out to fight against us"

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "came out to meet us for battle" (yatsa liqratenu la-milchamah — "came out to meet us for/to battle"); LOGOS: "came out against us for battle"; PNEUMA: "came out to fight against us." The Hebrew liqratenu is "to meet us" — EMET is most literal. (2) EMET/LOGOS: "king of Heshbon/Cheshbon" — title retained; PNEUMA: "king of Heshbon" — drops formal title style. (3) EMET: "struck them" (nakkem); LOGOS: "struck them down"; PNEUMA: "defeated them." **Resolution:** "Sihon the king of Heshbon and Og the king of Bashan came out to meet us for battle, and we struck them" — EMET; "came out to meet" is the proper rendering of qara and "struck" preserves nakah.

---

## V.7/8 — "Inheritance" recipients: tribal vs. clan designation

- **EMET:** "gave it as an inheritance to Re'uven and to Gad and to the half tribe of Menasheh"
- **LOGOS:** "gave it for an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of the Manassites"
- **PNEUMA:** "gave it as an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh"

**Differences:** EMET uses Hebrew name forms (Re'uven, Gad, Menasheh) with "to Re'uven and to Gad" preserving the Hebrew prepositional structure. LOGOS/PNEUMA use Anglicized gentilic forms ("Reubenites, Gadites"). LOGOS: "half-tribe of the Manassites" — unusual English form. PNEUMA: "half-tribe of Manasseh" — cleaner. **Resolution:** "gave it as an inheritance to Reuben and to Gad and to the half-tribe of Manasseh" — retains EMET's prepositional structure with English name forms per project convention.

---

## V.8/9 — "Keep...and do them" vs. "Therefore keep" vs. "Carefully follow"

- **EMET:** "And you shall keep the words of this covenant and do them, so that you may act wisely [taskilu] in all that you do."
- **LOGOS:** "Therefore keep the words of this covenant and do them, that you may prosper in all that you do."
- **PNEUMA:** "Carefully follow the terms of this covenant, so that you may prosper in everything you do."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "keep the words of this covenant and do them" — Hebrew ushertem et-divrei ha-brit ha-zot va'asitem otam — "keep the words... and do them." LOGOS retains this double formula; PNEUMA collapses to "Carefully follow the terms." The Hebrew two-verb structure is significant. (2) EMET: "act wisely" for tashkilu (from sakal — to be wise/prudent/successful); LOGOS/PNEUMA: "prosper." "Prosper" is idiomatic but loses the wisdom nuance of sakal. (3) EMET: "in all that you do"; LOGOS: same; PNEUMA: "in everything you do" — minor variation. (4) EMET: "And you shall keep" — connects to prior verse; LOGOS: "Therefore keep" — adds a causal inference; PNEUMA: drops the connective. **Resolution:** "And you shall keep the words of this covenant and do them, so that you may act wisely in all that you do" — EMET; preserves the double verb and the wisdom nuance of sakal.

---

## V.9/10 — "Chiefs" vs. "heads" vs. "leaders"

- **EMET:** "your chiefs, your tribes, your elders, your officers, every man of Yisra'el"
- **LOGOS:** "the heads of your tribes, your elders, and your officers, all the men of Israel"
- **PNEUMA:** "your leaders and chief men, your elders and officials, and all the other men of Israel"

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "your chiefs" for raisheichem; LOGOS: "the heads of your tribes"; PNEUMA: "your leaders and chief men." The Hebrew raisheichem is "your heads/chiefs" — LOGOS captures the tribal-headship meaning best. (2) EMET: "your tribes" listed separately, creating a five-item list; LOGOS integrates "tribes" with "heads." The Hebrew sheivetichem ("your tribes") may be in apposition to raisheichem. (3) PNEUMA: "officials" for shotereichem (officers); EMET/LOGOS: "officers." Shoter is a term for officer/magistrate, not merely "official." **Resolution:** "the heads of your tribes, your elders, and your officers, all the men of Israel" — LOGOS; the tribal-head reading and "officers" for shoter are most accurate.

---

## V.10/11 — "Sojourner" vs. "foreigner" / "within your camps" vs. "in your camp"

- **EMET:** "your sojourner who is within your camps, from the hewer of your wood to the drawer of your water"
- **LOGOS:** "the sojourner who is in your camp, from the one who chops your wood to the one who draws your water"
- **PNEUMA:** "the foreigners living in your camps who chop your wood and carry your water"

**Differences:** (1) EMET/LOGOS: "sojourner" (ger) — the established project term; PNEUMA: "foreigners" — see project conventions establishing "sojourner" for ger. (2) EMET: "within your camps" (plural — b'qerev machaneicha); LOGOS: "in your camp" (singular); PNEUMA: "in your camps" (plural). The Hebrew has a plural. (3) EMET: "hewer of your wood" — literal; LOGOS: "one who chops your wood"; PNEUMA: "who chop your wood." The Hebrew chotzev atzeicha ("hewer of your wood") is a participial expression — "hewer" is the most literal and preserves the archaic character of the phrase. (4) EMET: "drawer of your water"; LOGOS: "one who draws your water"; PNEUMA: "carry your water" — PNEUMA loses the specific Hebrew shov ei mayim ("drawers of water"). **Resolution:** "your sojourner who is within your camps, from the hewer of your wood to the drawer of your water" — EMET; "sojourner," plural "camps," and "hewer/drawer" preserve the Hebrew precisely.

---

## V.11/12 — "Oath" (alah) — translation and presentation

- **EMET:** "to enter into the covenant of the LORD your God and into his oath [alah] that the LORD your God is making with you today"
- **LOGOS:** "so that you may enter into the sworn covenant of the LORD your God, which the LORD your God is making with you today"
- **PNEUMA:** "You are standing here in order to enter into a covenant with the LORD your God, a covenant the LORD is making with you this day and sealing with an oath"

**Differences:** (1) The Hebrew has two items: ha-brit (the covenant) and alah (the oath/curse). EMET preserves both as separate objects. LOGOS collapses them into "sworn covenant." PNEUMA renders the covenant first, then appends "sealing with an oath." (2) EMET: "his oath [alah]" — with gloss; alah can mean oath or curse — a deliberate ambiguity. LOGOS's "sworn covenant" loses this. (3) PNEUMA adds "sealing with" — not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew is simply "and into his oath." **Resolution:** "to enter into the covenant of the LORD your God and into his oath that the LORD your God is making with you today" — EMET (without gloss in main text); preserves both covenant and oath as distinct elements.

---

## V.12/13 — "Establish you today as his people" — phrasing

- **EMET:** "in order to establish you today as his people, and that he may be your God, as he spoke to you and as he swore to your fathers"
- **LOGOS:** "that he may establish you today as his people, and that he may be your God, as he promised you, and as he swore to your fathers"
- **PNEUMA:** "to confirm you this day as his people, that he may be your God as he promised you and as he swore to your ancestors, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "as he spoke to you" (ka'asher diber lakh); LOGOS: "as he promised you"; PNEUMA: "as he promised you." The Hebrew diber means "spoke" — not "promised." EMET is literal; LOGOS/PNEUMA interpret the speech-act as a promise. (2) PNEUMA: "ancestors" for avoteicha; EMET/LOGOS: "fathers." Project convention uses "fathers" for avot in patriarchal contexts. (3) All three list the three patriarchs; PNEUMA uses modern English "ancestors" — departure from convention. **Resolution:** "in order to establish you today as his people, and that he may be your God, as he spoke to you and as he swore to your fathers — to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob" — EMET; "spoke" over "promised" and "fathers" per convention.

---

## V.13/14 — "This covenant and this oath" vs. "this sworn covenant"

- **EMET:** "And not with you alone am I making this covenant and this oath"
- **LOGOS:** "It is not with you alone that I am making this sworn covenant"
- **PNEUMA:** "I am making this covenant, with its oath, not only with you"

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "this covenant and this oath" (ha-brit ha-zot ve-et ha-alah ha-zot) — preserves both nouns with demonstrative adjectives on each. LOGOS collapses to "this sworn covenant." PNEUMA: "this covenant, with its oath" — treats the oath as subordinate to the covenant. (2) EMET opens with "And not with you alone" — fronting the exclusive negation; LOGOS uses formal inversion; PNEUMA places "not only with you" after the main clause. **Resolution:** "And not with you alone am I making this covenant and this oath" — EMET; both nouns should be preserved as the Hebrew clearly has two distinct objects.

---

## V.14/15 — "Whoever is not here with us today"

- **EMET:** "but with whoever is standing here with us today before the LORD our God, and also with whoever is not here with us today"
- **LOGOS:** "but with whoever is standing here with us today before the LORD our God, and with whoever is not here with us today"
- **PNEUMA:** "who are standing here with us today in the presence of the LORD our God but also with those who are not here today"

**Differences:** (1) EMET/LOGOS: "whoever is not here with us today" — closer to the Hebrew asher eynenu poh imanu ha-yom; PNEUMA: "those who are not here today" — drops "with us." The "with us" (imanu) is present in Hebrew and theologically significant. (2) PNEUMA: "in the presence of the LORD our God" — idiomatic; EMET/LOGOS: "before the LORD our God" — more literal rendering of lifnei. (3) EMET: "also with whoever" adds "also" not explicitly in MT at that point; LOGOS lacks it. **Resolution:** "but with whoever is standing here with us today before the LORD our God, and with whoever is not here with us today" — LOGOS; "with us" retained, "before" over "in the presence of."

---

## V.15/16 — "Dwelt" vs. "lived" / "passed through the midst"

- **EMET:** "for you know how we dwelt in the land of Mitsrayim, and how we passed through the midst of the nations through whom you passed"
- **LOGOS:** "You know how we lived in the land of Egypt, and how we came through the midst of the nations through which you passed"
- **PNEUMA:** "You yourselves know how we lived in Egypt and how we passed through the countries on the way here."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "dwelt" (yashavnu — to dwell/sit/remain); LOGOS/PNEUMA: "lived." "Dwelt" is the more precise rendering of yashav. (2) EMET: "passed through the midst" (v'na'avor b'qerev); LOGOS: "came through the midst"; PNEUMA: "passed through the countries" — PNEUMA drops "midst" (b'qerev). (3) PNEUMA: "on the way here" — an addition not in the Hebrew. (4) EMET adds "for" as a causal connector; LOGOS/PNEUMA begin with "You know." **Resolution:** "for you know how we dwelt in the land of Egypt, and how we passed through the midst of the nations through whom you passed" — EMET; "dwelt," "passed through the midst," and the causal "for" are all supported by the Hebrew.

---

## V.16/17 — "Detestable things" vs. "detestable images" / "idols" enumeration

- **EMET:** "and you saw their detestable things and their idols — wood and stone, silver and gold — which were among them"
- **LOGOS:** "And you have seen their detestable things, their idols of wood and stone, of silver and gold, which were among them"
- **PNEUMA:** "You saw among them their detestable images and idols of wood and stone, of silver and gold."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "their detestable things" (shiqutzeichem — their abominations/detestable things) — plural noun; LOGOS: "their detestable things" — same; PNEUMA: "their detestable images" — adds "images" not in the Hebrew. (2) EMET: dash before "wood and stone" preserving the appositive listing; LOGOS: "of wood and stone, of silver and gold" — uses "of" as appositive preposition. (3) PNEUMA: "which were among them" is dropped. **Resolution:** "and you saw their detestable things and their idols — wood and stone, silver and gold — which were among them" — EMET; "detestable things" is precise for shiqutzim and the appositive dash preserves the listing structure.

---

## V.17/18 — "Lest there be" (warning formula) / "root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit"

- **EMET:** "Lest there be among you a man or woman or family or tribe whose heart is turning away today from the LORD our God, to go and serve the gods of those nations — lest there be among you a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit [rosh ve-la'anah]"
- **LOGOS:** "Beware lest there be among you a man or woman or clan or tribe whose heart is turning away today from the LORD our God to go and serve the gods of those nations. Beware lest there be among you a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit"
- **PNEUMA:** "Make sure there is no man or woman, clan or tribe among you today whose heart turns away from the LORD our God to go and worship the gods of those nations; make sure there is no root among you that produces such bitter poison."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "Lest there be" — literal pen-yesh construction; LOGOS: "Beware lest there be" — adds "Beware" for the warning tone of pen; PNEUMA: "Make sure there is no" — changes to a positive command structure, obscuring the Hebrew construction. (2) EMET: "family" for mishpachah; LOGOS/PNEUMA: "clan." "Clan" is the more accurate anthropological term for mishpachah. (3) The poisonous root: EMET: "bearing poisonous and bitter fruit [rosh ve-la'anah]" with gloss; LOGOS: "bearing poisonous and bitter fruit" (no gloss); PNEUMA: "that produces such bitter poison" — "such" is an addition, and "bitter poison" collapses the two-term merism (rosh + la'anah). (4) PNEUMA: "worship the gods" for la'avod — "serve" is more literal for avad. **Resolution:** "Lest there be among you a man or woman or clan or tribe whose heart is turning away today from the LORD our God, to go and serve the gods of those nations — lest there be among you a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit" — EMET structure and vocabulary, with "clan" for mishpachah.

---

## V.18/19 — "I shall have peace" vs. "I shall be safe" / cryptic watered/thirsty idiom

- **EMET:** "he blesses himself in his heart, saying: I shall have peace, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart — in order to add the watered [to] the thirsty [one]"
- **LOGOS:** "blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart.' This would lead to the sweeping away of moist and dry alike."
- **PNEUMA:** "they invoke a blessing on themselves, thinking, 'I will be safe, even though I persist in going my own stubborn way' — this will bring disaster on the well-watered land as well as the dry."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "I shall have peace" (shalom li — "peace to me"); LOGOS/PNEUMA: "I shall be safe." The Hebrew shalom li is literally "there is peace to me" — EMET's "I shall have peace" is the closer rendering. "Safe" is interpretive. (2) EMET: "walk in the stubbornness of my heart" (be-sheririut libi elekh) — literal; LOGOS: "walk in the stubbornness of my heart" — same; PNEUMA: "persist in going my own stubborn way" — paraphrase. (3) The cryptic closing idiom (lesafot ha-ravah et ha-tsemah): EMET: "in order to add the watered to the thirsty" — most literal but opaque; LOGOS: "the sweeping away of moist and dry alike" — interpretive but coherent; PNEUMA: "disaster on the well-watered land as well as the dry" — renders abstractly with "land." The Hebrew is genuinely obscure; LOGOS's rendering ("sweeping away") captures the destructive sense without being as abstract as PNEUMA. **Resolution:** "he blesses himself in his heart, saying: I shall have peace, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart — sweeping away the watered along with the thirsty" — EMET's "have peace" and "stubbornness," LOGOS's interpretive sense for the idiom.

---

## V.19/20 — "Smoke against" / "curse written in this scroll" vs. "book"

- **EMET:** "the anger of the LORD and his jealousy shall smoke against that man, and all the curse [alah] written in this scroll shall lie upon him"
- **LOGOS:** "the anger of the LORD and his jealousy will smoke against that man, and every curse written in this book will settle on him"
- **PNEUMA:** "his wrath and zeal will burn against them. All the curses written in this book will fall on them"

**Differences:** (1) EMET/LOGOS: "anger of the LORD and his jealousy" — two distinct nouns (af + qin'ah); PNEUMA: "wrath and zeal" — "zeal" for qin'ah is unusual and weaker than "jealousy" in a covenant context. (2) EMET/LOGOS: "smoke against" (ve-anenu) — the verb ana' means to smoke/fume; PNEUMA: "burn against" — loses the specific smoke imagery. (3) EMET: "all the curse [alah]" — singular, with gloss; LOGOS: "every curse" (singular rendering); PNEUMA: "all the curses" — pluralizes. The Hebrew ha-alah is singular. (4) EMET: "this scroll" (ha-sefer ha-zeh); LOGOS/PNEUMA: "this book." Sefer can be scroll or book; "scroll" is more precise for a Torah context. (5) EMET: "shall lie upon him" (revatsah bo); LOGOS: "will settle on him" — both render the verb. (6) PNEUMA switches to plural pronoun ("them") for the single offender — smoothing, but departing from the Hebrew singular focus. **Resolution:** "the anger of the LORD and his jealousy shall smoke against that man, and all the curse written in this scroll shall lie upon him" — EMET; "jealousy" over "zeal," "smoke" over "burn," singular "curse," and "scroll" over "book."

---

## V.20/21 — "Single out for disaster" / "Book of the Torah" vs. "Book of the Instruction"

- **EMET:** "And the LORD will single him out from all the tribes of Yisra'el for disaster, according to all the curses of the covenant written in this scroll of the Torah."
- **LOGOS:** "And the LORD will single him out from all the tribes of Israel for calamity, in accordance with all the curses of the covenant written in this Book of the Instruction."
- **PNEUMA:** "The LORD will single them out from all the tribes of Israel for disaster, according to all the curses of the covenant written in this Book of the Instruction."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "for disaster" (le-ra'ah); LOGOS: "for calamity"; PNEUMA: "for disaster" — EMET/PNEUMA agree; "disaster" is the more common translation of ra'ah in this context. (2) EMET: "scroll of the Torah"; LOGOS/PNEUMA: "Book of the Instruction." The Hebrew sefer ha-torah — LOGOS and PNEUMA use "Instruction" consistently for torah following the DEU_028 convention. "Instruction" is the ruling established for torah in this project (see memory). (3) PNEUMA: "them" (plural) for a single individual — pronoun smoothing. **Resolution:** "And the LORD will single him out from all the tribes of Israel for disaster, according to all the curses of the covenant written in this Book of the Instruction" — LOGOS; "disaster" over "calamity" and "Book of the Instruction" follows established convention.

---

## V.21/22 — "Next generation" vs. "generation to come" / "plagues" vs. "afflictions" vs. "calamities"

- **EMET:** "And the next generation, your sons who rise up after you, and the foreigner who comes from a distant land, shall say when they see the plagues of that land and the sicknesses with which the LORD has made it sick"
- **LOGOS:** "And the generation to come, your children who rise up after you, and the foreigner who comes from a far land, will see the afflictions of that land and the sicknesses with which the LORD has made it sick"
- **PNEUMA:** "Your children who follow you in later generations and foreigners who come from distant lands will see the calamities that have fallen on the land and the diseases with which the LORD has afflicted it."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "next generation" (ha-dor ha-acharon); LOGOS: "generation to come" — both reasonable; PNEUMA: "later generations" (pluralizes). The Hebrew ha-dor is singular. (2) EMET: "your sons" (beneichem); LOGOS: "your children"; PNEUMA: "your children." "Sons" is the literal Hebrew. (3) EMET: "plagues" (chalayim); LOGOS: "afflictions"; PNEUMA: "calamities." The Hebrew chalayim means sicknesses/diseases; "plagues" is slightly different from chalayim but captures the severity. LOGOS: "afflictions" is accurate. (4) EMET: "sicknesses with which the LORD has made it sick" (machaluyim asher chilah YHWH bah) — the paronomasia (sickness/sick) is in the Hebrew; LOGOS preserves it; PNEUMA: "diseases with which the LORD has afflicted it" — loses the word-play. **Resolution:** "And the generation to come, your sons who rise up after you, and the foreigner who comes from a far land, will see the afflictions of that land and the sicknesses with which the LORD has made it sick" — LOGOS structure with "sons" from EMET and "afflictions" from LOGOS.

## V.22/23 — Desolation description: "sulfur and salt" vs. "brimstone and salt" / word order

- **EMET:** "all its soil [is] sulfur and salt, burned over — it is not sown and does not sprout and no grass grows in it — like the overthrow of Sedom and 'Amorah, Admah and Tsevoyim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and in his wrath"
- **LOGOS:** "the whole land burned out with brimstone and salt, nothing sown and nothing growing, where no plant sprouts, an overthrow like that of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and wrath"
- **PNEUMA:** "The whole land will be a burning waste of salt and sulfur — nothing planted, nothing sprouting, no vegetation growing on it. It will be like the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboyim, which the LORD overthrew in fierce anger."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "sulfur" (gofrit); LOGOS: "brimstone" — the archaic synonym; PNEUMA: "sulfur." "Sulfur" is the modern English; "brimstone" is traditional. EMET/PNEUMA: "sulfur and salt" preserves the Hebrew order (gofrit va-melach). LOGOS: "brimstone and salt" — different order. PNEUMA inverts to "salt and sulfur." The Hebrew order is gofrit (sulfur) then melach (salt). (2) EMET: "its soil" (admatahy); LOGOS: "the whole land"; PNEUMA: "the whole land." The Hebrew kol artzah could be "all its land/soil." (3) Three-part negation: EMET: "not sown and does not sprout and no grass grows"; LOGOS: "nothing sown and nothing growing, where no plant sprouts"; PNEUMA: "nothing planted, nothing sprouting, no vegetation growing." EMET follows the Hebrew three-part structure (lo tizara ve-lo tatsmiah ve-lo ya'aleh). (4) EMET: "like the overthrow" (ke-mahpekhat); LOGOS: "an overthrow like that of"; PNEUMA: "like the destruction" — PNEUMA loses the specific Hebrew mahpekhat ("overthrow/overturning"). (5) PNEUMA: "in fierce anger" — adds "fierce" not in the Hebrew for the first anger term (b'apo). **Resolution:** "all its land is sulfur and salt, burned over — it is not sown and does not sprout and no grass grows in it — like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and in his wrath" — EMET structure, English place names per convention, "sulfur" over "brimstone."

## V.23/24 — "Greatness of this burning anger" vs. "heat of this great anger"

- **EMET:** "What is the greatness of this burning anger?"
- **LOGOS:** "What caused the heat of this great anger?"
- **PNEUMA:** "Why this fierce, burning anger?"

**Differences:** The Hebrew meh chori ha-af ha-gadol ha-zeh — "what [is] the fierceness of this great anger?" (1) EMET: "greatness of this burning anger" — inverts adjective placement; chori means heat/burning. (2) LOGOS: "What caused the heat of this great anger?" — adds "caused" which is not in the Hebrew. (3) PNEUMA: "Why this fierce, burning anger?" — drops "great" and conflates into a simpler question. **Resolution:** "What is the fierceness of this great burning anger?" — a blend capturing chori (heat/fierceness), gadol (great), and the Hebrew question form without adding "caused."

## V.24/25 — "Forsook" vs. "abandoned" / "covenant of the LORD"

- **EMET:** "Because they forsook the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers, which he made with them when he brought them out from the land of Mitsrayim"
- **LOGOS:** "It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers, which he made with them when he brought them out of the land of Egypt"
- **PNEUMA:** "It is because this people abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their ancestors, the covenant he made with them when he brought them out of Egypt."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "forsook" (azav); LOGOS/PNEUMA: "abandoned." Both are valid for azav; "forsook" is more formal and traditional. (2) PNEUMA: "this people" — adds the demonstrative not in the Hebrew at this point. (3) PNEUMA: "ancestors" for avotam; EMET/LOGOS: "fathers" — project convention maintains "fathers" for avot. (4) PNEUMA: "the covenant he made" repeats "the covenant" — the Hebrew does not have a second "covenant" here. **Resolution:** "Because they forsook the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers, which he made with them when he brought them out from the land of Egypt" — EMET's "forsook" and "fathers," LOGOS's "Egypt" per English name convention.

## V.25/26 — "Went and served" / "gods whom he had not allotted to them"

- **EMET:** "and they went and served other gods and bowed down to them — gods whom they had not known and whom he had not allotted to them"
- **LOGOS:** "and went and served other gods and worshiped them, gods whom they had not known and whom he had not allotted to them"
- **PNEUMA:** "They went off and worshiped other gods and bowed down to them — gods they did not know, gods he had not given them."

**Differences:** (1) EMET/LOGOS: "served other gods" (va-ya'avdu); PNEUMA: "worshiped other gods" — avad is "serve," not specifically "worship." "Served" is the more accurate and theologically weighted term. (2) EMET: "bowed down to them" (va-yishtachu); LOGOS: "worshiped them" — LOGOS uses "worshiped" for the second verb, losing the prostration meaning of shachah. PNEUMA renders correctly: "bowed down to them." (3) PNEUMA: "gods they did not know, gods he had not given them" — PNEUMA's "given" for chalaq (allotted/apportioned) weakens the covenant-distribution language; EMET/LOGOS: "allotted" is more precise. **Resolution:** "and they went and served other gods and bowed down to them — gods whom they had not known and whom he had not allotted to them" — EMET; "served," "bowed down," and "allotted" are each the most precise renderings.

## V.26/27 — "Burned against that land" / "all the curse"

- **EMET:** "And the anger of the LORD burned against that land to bring upon it all the curse [alah] written in this scroll."
- **LOGOS:** "Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against this land, bringing upon it all the curses written in this book"
- **PNEUMA:** "Therefore the LORD's anger burned against this land, so that he brought on it all the curses written in this book."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "burned against that land" (chara af-YHWH ba-aretz ha-hi); LOGOS: "was kindled against this land" — switches "that land" to "this land" — but the Hebrew ha-aretz ha-hi is "that land" (third-person demonstrative), not "this land." PNEUMA: "against this land" — same error. EMET is correct. (2) EMET: "all the curse" (singular ha-alah); LOGOS/PNEUMA: "all the curses" (plural). See v.19/20 note — ha-alah is singular. (3) EMET: "this scroll"; LOGOS/PNEUMA: "this book." **Resolution:** "And the anger of the LORD burned against that land to bring upon it all the curse written in this scroll" — EMET; "that land," singular "curse," and "scroll."

## V.27/28 — "Uprooted" / "anger and wrath and great fury" triad

- **EMET:** "And the LORD uprooted them from upon their land in anger and in wrath and in great fury, and cast them into another land, as it is this day."
- **LOGOS:** "and the LORD uprooted them from their land in anger and fury and great wrath, and cast them into another land, as they are today."
- **PNEUMA:** "In furious anger and in great wrath the LORD uprooted them from their land and thrust them into another land, as it is now."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: triad "in anger and in wrath and in great fury" (b'af u-v'chemah u-v'qetsef gadol) — EMET preserves preposition on each; LOGOS: "in anger and fury and great wrath" — different ordering of the three nouns (chemah and qetsef); the Hebrew order is af (anger), chemah (wrath/fury), qetsef (indignation/fury). LOGOS inverts chemah and qetsef. PNEUMA: merges into "furious anger and in great wrath" — drops af entirely. (2) PNEUMA: "thrust them" for va-yashlichem; EMET/LOGOS: "cast them" — both render the verb; "cast" is more standard. (3) EMET: "as it is this day"; LOGOS: "as they are today" — slightly different construction; PNEUMA: "as it is now" — drops "this day" (ha-yom ha-zeh). **Resolution:** "And the LORD uprooted them from their land in anger and in wrath and in great fury, and cast them into another land, as it is this day" — EMET; full triad with prepositions, "cast," and "this day."

## V.28/29 — "Hidden things" / "revealed things" / "sons" vs. "children" / "Torah" vs. "instruction"

- **EMET:** "The hidden things belong to the LORD our God [ha-nistarot la-YHWH Eloheinu], but the revealed things [belong] to us and to our sons forever — to do all the words of this Torah."
- **LOGOS:** "The hidden things belong to the LORD our God, but the revealed things belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this instruction."
- **PNEUMA:** "The hidden things belong to the LORD our God, but the revealed things belong to us and to our children forever, that we may follow all the words of this instruction."

**Differences:** (1) EMET: "our sons" (veneinu); LOGOS/PNEUMA: "our children." The Hebrew veneinu is literally "our sons" — the same masculine plural used throughout for generational transmission. EMET preserves this; LOGOS/PNEUMA use the gender-neutral "children." (2) EMET: "to our sons forever — to do all the words of this Torah"; LOGOS: "to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this instruction"; PNEUMA: "to our children forever, that we may follow all the words of this instruction." PNEUMA: "follow" for la'asot (to do) — "do" is the more literal rendering. (3) EMET: "Torah" (ha-torah ha-zot — "this Torah"); LOGOS/PNEUMA: "instruction." Per the project memory note, the ruling for DEU has been "instruction" for torah. **Resolution:** "The hidden things belong to the LORD our God, but the revealed things belong to us and to our sons forever — to do all the words of this instruction" — EMET's "sons" (literal) and "do" (literal), LOGOS/PNEUMA's "instruction" (established convention for DEU torah).
